protections: WebSocket handshake admission: an upgrade request to the web UI event socket must be authorisation- and origin-checked before upgrader.Upgrade, admitting same-origin browsers, excluding foreign Origins, and still admitting Origin-less non-browser clients (server/websockets/client.go:114-141, server/server.go:199,333-336).

Origin/path policy consistency: any decision keyed on the request path (the CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin grant and the HTML-preview rule) must use the path the router actually matched (decoded r.URL.Path, without the query string), not the raw percent-encoded r.RequestURI (server/server.go:286-295).

Basic-auth enforcement must be decided per request from state the request cannot clear process-wide; handlers must not switch UI credentials off for other in-flight requests (server/server.go:216-253,297-312; internal/auth/auth.go:11-20).

Origin validation for state-changing HTTP endpoints: CORS response headers do not stop cross-origin simple POSTs, so send/release must reject foreign Origins themselves (server/server.go:162-176,267-325; server/apiv1/send.go:45-59; server/apiv1/release.go:58-101).

CORS preflight exemption: only genuine, credential-less preflight OPTIONS requests may skip basic auth; the exemption must stay narrow enough to preserve that documented behaviour (server/server.go:299, CHANGELOG.md:215).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The line carries an explicit comment ('allow multi-domain') and overrides gorilla's default same-origin check deliberately; Mailpit is a local development mail catcher, the handshake carries no stored data, and the socket only pushes notifications.

ServeWs performs its own BasicAuth check (client.go:115-127), so the route deliberately does not use middleWareFunc; every other UI/API route is wrapped in it, and the handler is treated as self-contained.

The condition only *adds* an Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header, so a raw/decoded mismatch fails closed: an encoded path still routes, but it simply does not receive the CORS grant. The regex ends in \.html$ and is applied to a string that still carries the query string, which likewise only narrows the grant.

Browsers never attach credentials to a CORS preflight, so skipping auth for OPTIONS is required for --api-cors to work at all (the changelog records it as an intentional fix), and the only OPTIONS handler reachable through the middleware returns a blank 200 with no body or side effect (apiv1/api.go:76-80); the exemption has no exploitable consequence.

The mutation is scoped to the send endpoint, the deferred restore runs immediately after the handler returns, and server_test.go:455-492 asserts that regular API endpoints are not affected by send API auth settings; the code reads as deliberate request-scoped plumbing.

Mailpit's API is unauthenticated by default and exists to be driven by local scripts and CI; the CORS policy (and the browser's preflight) is assumed to cover cross-origin abuse, the handlers ignore Content-Type so any client shape works, and release additionally requires SMTP relaying to be configured.

masking: T5 is invisible unless UI auth is configured: with auth.UICredentials == nil the gates at server/server.go:300 and server/websockets/client.go:115 are no-ops, so the race only matters on an authenticated deployment.
T3 is reachable only when --api-cors is set, because the whole CORS block at server/server.go:290 is skipped otherwise.

T4 has an effect only for OPTIONS requests matched by the api/v1 OPTIONS route (server/server.go:202); any other method/path is answered by the mux 405 handler before middleWareFunc runs, so the exemption exposes no handler.
T6's release vector requires SMTP relay configuration (server/apiv1/release.go:170); the send vector is always available and stores a message.

conflicts.what: The natural same-origin rule (compare the Origin host with r.Host) rejects the cross-origin UI deployment that the Access-Control-Allow-Origin policy at server/server.go:290-295 exists to support; an origin check must also admit the configured AccessControlAllowOrigin value and reverse-proxied public hosts, so a strict host equality fix breaks a must-keep-working configuration.

Requiring an Origin header, or credentials, on unsafe HTTP methods also catches CORS preflight, which browsers send without credentials; the OPTIONS exemption at server/server.go:299 has to survive any global origin/auth middleware or --api-cors breaks.

Replacing the global auth.UICredentials toggle with per-request credentials must keep both Send API auth modes working (server_test.go:336-414) while the websocket gate at server/websockets/client.go:115 still sees the real UI credentials; a naive fix that stops clearing the global changes send-API behaviour, and a fix that keeps clearing it leaves the websocket gate blind during the window.

fairness_risks: Origin-less clients are legitimate: gorilla only consults CheckOrigin when an Origin header is present, and scripts/proxies/CLI websocket clients normally send none. A rule that rejects missing Origin would refuse a legitimate input shape and break non-browser use.

The web UI itself must keep connecting: AppNotifications.vue:35 builds the socket URL from document.location.host and AppNotifications.vue:50 opens it with no headers; with --webroot the endpoint is Webroot+'api/events' (server/server.go:199), so a check hardcoding /api/events breaks webroot deployments.
Reverse-proxy deployments (Vite/nginx in front of Mailpit) have Origin = the public host and r.Host = the backend address; exact Origin == scheme://r.Host comparison refuses a legitimate deployment.
--api-cors is an existing supported flag, including a literal '*'; a security rule that refuses wildcard or configured cross-origin values contradicts a documented feature.
CORS preflight must stay credential-less (server/server.go:299, CHANGELOG.md:215); requiring auth or an Origin on OPTIONS breaks cross-origin API use.

The API is intentionally unauthenticated by default and is called by local scripts and CI without an Origin header or a JSON Content-Type; a blanket 'reject cross-origin/no-Origin POST' rule refuses legitimate use, and send.go:45-52 deliberately ignores Content-Type.

Browser clients cannot set an Authorization header on a WebSocket handshake (AppNotifications.vue:50; client.go:116 relies on r.BasicAuth()), so the websocket authenticates only via cached Basic credentials; a fix that requires a token header on the handshake breaks the UI.

design.why: The strongest available stack is four independent judgement points. T1+T2 form one guard (the websocket admission path) but hide two decisions: the CheckOrigin override at client.go:37 must be replaced with a real check, and the /api/events route is registered outside middleWareFunc (server.go:199), so a fix placed only in the shared middleware leaves the reported socket open; their dismiss reasons differ (the deliberate multi-domain comment versus 'ServeWs does its own auth'). T3 is a separate site and a separate decision: the raw RequestURI path policy at server.go:287-291 must be evaluated on the decoded, query-free path, otherwise any path-gated origin check copied from it inherits the percent-encoded-path bypass the advisory names. T6 is a separate sink family: state-changing POSTs (send, release) have no origin validation at all, so a websocket-only fix still lets a foreign page trigger them; its dismiss reason ('CORS/preflight handles it, the API is open by design') is unlike the other two. That mix covers a deepseek-type (T2, T6), a mimo-type/hows-type (T3), and coupled values (the --api-cors origin, webroot and Origin-less clients that the T1 fix must keep working). T5 is a real fifth group but a concurrency race makes hidden tests flaky; T4 is kept as a fairness/conflict constraint rather than a scored trap because the only reachable OPTIONS handler returns a blank 200. If the harness only accepts advisory-named surfaces, the stack narrows to T1/T2 plus T3, which is still two independent edits in two packages.

The tree contains no websocket Origin check at all (grep for Origin/CheckOrigin finds only client.go:37 and the CORS config), so whatever A added is not identifiable at this pin.

history.a_fix_leaves_b_open is answered true on this reading: the only refusal logic in the tree lives in middleWareFunc (server.go:267-325) and the /api/events route is registered without it (server.go:199), so an earlier path/origin policy of that shape cannot cover the socket. If A's fix was instead a CheckOrigin implementation that a later commit reverted, the answer would be 'A's code is not present' rather than 'A leaves B open'; the pinned content cannot distinguish the two.

history.b_in_code_a_wrote is left null: client.go is the original Gorilla-derived handler (client.go:1-5) with a long-standing unconditional CheckOrigin, which suggests B is not in code A wrote, but A's patch was not readable.

T3's security direction is uncertain: in the current code the raw-vs-decoded mismatch at server.go:291 fails closed (the request is routed but receives no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header), so on its own it leaks nothing. It is recorded because the advisory names percent-encoded paths and because this line is the obvious template a solver would copy for a path-gated Origin check, where the same shape would fail open. A hidden test that only exercises the CORS header would not prove a vulnerability.

Whether the hidden tests exercise T5 (credential race) or T6 (HTTP CSRF on send/release) is unknown: both are repo-level gaps not named by the candidate summary; they are recorded as uncovered_upstream rather than advisory_route.

gorilla/mux route matching and path cleaning are assumed from its documented default because the dependency source is not vendored in the worktree; no UseEncodedPath or SkipClean call exists in this repository, so r.URL.Path is decoded before matching and the percent-encoded forms reach the same handlers.
The candidate is labelled H3b2 in the run inputs; the output schema enumerates only H3a/H3b/H3c, so pattern is reported as H3b.

Mailpit's default deployment is unauthenticated and localhost-bound; every trap's real-world exploitability therefore depends on the deployment exposing the UI/API beyond localhost, which the code itself does not enforce.
